\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare \system{} against representative single-modality validators on the
same fault suite (F1--F10).
\textbf{istioctl analyze}~\cite{istioctl-analyze} is the production static
analyzer for Istio (reported in offline mode, \texttt{--use-kube=false}).
\textbf{Naive Dyn.} applies the candidate configuration and issues fixed HTTP
probes, flagging only coarse failure signals (e.g., elevated 5xx), without
policy-level assertions.
\textbf{Dyn.\ Only} is an ablation of \system{} that runs intent-driven traffic
validation without static modeling or result fusion; we use it as the dynamic
baseline because no public tool targets Istio traffic-policy semantics at the
same fault granularity.
\textbf{\system{} (Hybrid)} combines static modeling, orthogonal case
generation, and runtime consistency checking.

Table~\ref{tab:hybrid-effectiveness} summarizes detection outcomes on ten
representative misconfigurations spanning control-plane reference errors,
cross-resource policy conflicts, and runtime-only enforcement gaps.
\texttt{istioctl analyze} detects 2 of 10 cases (F1, F2), but misses intent-level and load-dependent faults (F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10).
Naive dynamic probing only flags coarse always-fail signals (F10).
Dyn.\ Only recovers runtime-exposed faults (F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F10) but misses purely static conflicts without a distinguishable traffic signature (F1, F2, F9).
Hybrid validation detects 10/10 cases by combining static cross-resource reasoning with policy-aware runtime checks, confirming that the two modalities are complementary and that fusion is necessary for full coverage.
